subject: History of USA
title: 13. War on Terror and Pakistan-USA Relations (2001–2012)

segments.text: Pakistan and the United States became close security partners after 9/11 but never had identical goals — this relationship should be described as strategic cooperation combined with persistent security divergence, never simply “alliance” or “enmity.” (See also History of Pakistan & India Topic 10 for Pakistan’s own foreign-policy perspective on this period.)
The U.S. invaded Afghanistan after 9/11 to destroy al-Qaeda and remove the Taliban government sheltering it, making Pakistan’s territory, airspace and intelligence cooperation highly important. Under

, Pakistan supported U.S. logistics, intelligence and counterterrorism efforts while receiving substantial assistance and, from 2004, major non-NATO ally status — but Pakistan itself faced growing militant violence, military operations in tribal areas, and political backlash over cooperation, meaning the relationship carried major internal costs, not only diplomatic ones.

Use a two-sided table: areas of cooperation and areas of conflict; explain the deeper structural problem — Washington prioritised counterterrorism/Afghanistan while Islamabad also focused on India, Afghan influence and domestic security.
Do not call Pakistan and the United States simple allies with identical objectives.
Do not describe the relationship only through aid figures; security interests and mutual mistrust matter more analytically.
Do not extend the topic beyond 2012 unless the question asks for later relations.
Pakistan became a major non-NATO U.S. ally in 2004.
U.S. forces killed Osama bin Laden in Abbottabad on 2 May 2011 without prior public Pakistani authorisation.
Pakistan closed NATO supply routes after the November 2011 Salala incident and reopened them in July 2012.
Describe the relationship as strategic cooperation combined with persistent security divergence — never simply “alliance” or “enmity.”
The 2011 trust crisis (Davis, Abbottabad, Salala) marks the clearest turning point toward open mutual distrust within the syllabus period.
